creative.body:
My colonoscopy came back clean.

Every inch of my colon, healthy, normal, no issues.

My doctor put the images down, looked at me, and said six words I haven't been able to stop thinking about.

"The problem was never your colon."

I'm going to tell you what she showed me on the next screen. I'm going to tell you what I almost did after that appointment that would have wasted another two months. And I'm going to tell you about the woman in my Mounjaro support group who waited three years before anyone said this to her, and what her stomach looks like now.

Because I learned something that day that I think every GLP-1 patient deserves to know on day one.

And almost nobody is being told.

I'd been on Mounjaro for nine months when I scheduled the colonoscopy. Not because anything scared me. Because I was tired. Tired of the bloating that turned every afternoon into a guessing game about which pants I could still button. Tired of going three, four, sometimes five days without a bowel movement. Tired of feeling like every meal I ate just parked itself inside me and stayed.

My doctor prescribed Mounjaro last January. For the weight. And it worked. I lost 34 pounds in six months. I fit into jeans I hadn't worn since my twenties. People at work started asking what I was doing. My sister said I looked ten years younger.

For the first time in as long as I can remember, I felt like I was winning.

But somewhere around month three, my stomach changed.

The bloating came first. By noon I'd be so distended I looked six months pregnant in the same jeans that had just started fitting again. I stopped wearing anything fitted. I stopped tucking shirts in. I started keeping a cardigan draped over my lap at my desk so nobody could see my waistband undone.

Then the constipation. Not the kind where you try and it's uncomfortable. The kind where nothing happens. At all. Your body just stops doing something it used to do without you even thinking about it. I'd go three days. Then four. I stopped counting because counting made it worse.

I bought Gas-X first. Then Dulcolax. Then Miralax because my doctor said it was gentle and I could take it daily. Then fiber gummies from Amazon because someone in my Mounjaro Facebook group swore by them. Then probiotics because the woman at Whole Foods said her whole gut changed in a week. Then magnesium citrate because a video on TikTok said it was the real answer.

Seven bottles on my bathroom counter. Every morning I'd stand there trying to figure out which combination might get me through the day.

None of it worked. The Gas-X would dull the pressure for an hour. Then it came right back. The Miralax would work once, maybe, then nothing for three more days. The fiber gummies made everything worse. The probiotics gave me cramps on top of everything else.

I stopped eating lunch. Not on purpose at first. I just couldn't face putting more food on top of food that hadn't moved. My husband would ask what I wanted for dinner and I'd feel my whole body tighten. Not hunger. Dread.

I finally had the thing that worked for the weight. And now I was afraid to eat.

I started skipping things. My sister's Sunday dinner. A friend's birthday at a restaurant downtown. A Saturday farmers market I used to love going to with my daughter. Not because I was in pain exactly. Because I never knew what was coming. The bloating. The pressure behind my ribs. The sulfur burps that would hit out of nowhere and smell like something had gone bad inside me.

My daughter was over for Sunday brunch in October and she was telling me about a trip her kids' school was planning to the apple orchard. She paused mid-sentence and said, "Mom, are you even listening?"

I wasn't.

I'd been calculating how many hours it had been since I'd eaten the half bagel in front of me, and whether the pressure I was already feeling meant my stomach hadn't moved that bagel along yet, and whether I could safely drink the coffee in front of me without making it worse.

She watched me come back to the conversation. She didn't say anything. She just looked at me for a second with the same look I used to give my own mother in her last year.

I told myself it was the trade-off. Lose the weight, lose your digestion. That's just what this costs.

Then one night I woke up at 2 AM with cramps so bad I thought something was actually wrong. I sat on the bathroom floor for forty minutes. Nothing happened. Nothing moved. I just sat there in the dark, sweating, waiting for it to pass.

That's when I called my gastroenterologist. Told her everything. She said let's do a colonoscopy, rule out anything structural.

So I did the prep. Drank the solution. Fasted for almost twenty hours. Went in.

When I woke up, she was standing there with images on the screen.

My colon was clean. No inflammation. No blockages. No polyps. Perfectly healthy tissue from one end to the other.

But she'd added an upper scope. And when she pulled those images up she got quiet.

"You see this?" She pointed at the screen. "This is food. Still in your stomach. From dinner two nights before the procedure."

Two nights. After twenty hours of fasting. Still sitting there. Barely broken down.

I stared at the screen. That was chicken. I could still see the shape of it. Chicken I'd eaten forty-four hours ago, sitting in my stomach like I'd swallowed it whole.

I felt my face get hot.

Nine months of pills and powders and fiber gummies and none of it mattered because the food wasn't even making it out of my stomach.

She pulled a stool over and sat down next to me.

"How many GLP-1 patients do you think I see in a week who are taking exactly what you're taking?" she asked.

"A lot?"

"Almost all of them. And almost all of them are getting worse. Because every product they're buying works on the wrong organ."

She turned the screen so I could see both sets of images side by side. My colon on the left. My stomach on the right.

"Your medication slows something called gastric emptying. It's doing exactly what it's designed to do for the weight. It slows the stomach down so you eat less and stay full longer. But when the stomach slows down that far, food doesn't move through. It sits. And when food sits in a stomach that's barely contracting, it starts to ferment. That fermentation produces gas. That's your bloating. That's your sulfur burps. That's the pressure behind your ribs every afternoon."

She pointed at my colon images. "This is healthy tissue. Your colon is doing exactly what it's supposed to do. It just has nothing to work with because the food is stuck upstream."

Then she said the part that I almost couldn't hear.

"I have a patient who came to me three years after starting Ozempic. She'd been doing exactly what you're doing. Buying laxatives. Drinking fiber. By the time she got to me, her stomach had been so chronically slowed for so long that the muscle had functionally stopped responding. The medical word is gastroparesis. We can manage it. We can't reverse it. She eats six small things a day now and she's never going back to a normal meal."

She let that sit for a second.

"I'm telling you this because nine months in is the window where this is still completely fixable. Two years in, sometimes. Three years, almost never. The longer you let your stomach sit at this kind of slowdown, the harder it gets to wake the muscle back up. Don't be the woman who waits."

I sat there with that.

I told her about everything I'd been taking. All seven bottles.

"None of that is going to help you," she said. "Your Miralax pulls water into the colon. Your Dulcolax stimulates the colon to contract. Your fiber gummies add bulk in the colon. Your probiotics colonize the colon." She tapped the screen. "This organ is fine. Everything you're taking works down here. Your problem is up here." She pointed back at my stomach.

"So what does my stomach actually need?"

"The first thing it needs is help contracting again. Your stomach muscles are still there. They still work. The medication is suppressing the signal that tells them to fire. There's a compound called apigenin. It's found naturally in celery juice. It acts as a prokinetic, which just means it supports the stomach's ability to contract and push food through even while the medication is slowing things down. That's the first thing you need. Without that, nothing else matters. The food just keeps sitting there."

"Why haven't I heard of that?"

"Because nobody is looking at the stomach. Everyone is looking at the colon. So every product on the market is built for the colon."

"Okay. What else?"

"Even once the stomach starts contracting again, you have weeks of fermentation gas trapped in there. That gas doesn't just disappear because digestion restarts. There's something called chlorophyllin that neutralizes fermentation gas directly. It breaks down what's already built up. That's the second piece. Apigenin gets the stomach moving. Chlorophyllin clears the gas that accumulated while it wasn't."

"And then what? Is that enough?"

"One more thing. Once the stomach is doing its job and the gas is handled, the colon still needs gentle support downstream. Not a stimulant. Not Dulcolax. Soluble prebiotic fiber. Just enough to keep things moving once the colon is actually receiving food properly again. The colon isn't your problem, but it still has to do its job once the upstream issue is fixed."

"Apigenin for the stomach. Chlorophyllin for the gas. Prebiotic fiber for the colon," I said. "Nothing on my counter does the first one. Nothing does the second one. They all skip straight to the third."

"That's exactly right. And that's why none of it has worked."

I left her office with the names of the three compounds written on the back of a parking garage receipt.

I drove straight to a vitamin shop on the way home and bought the first apigenin capsules I could find on the shelf. Then I went home and ordered standalone chlorophyllin from Amazon. Then I ordered prebiotic powder from another tab on the same site.

Three bottles. Three companies. Three different doses. About forty-eight dollars total.

I figured I'd just stack them. The doctor told me what the ingredients were. I'd find them myself for cheaper.

The first three weeks I felt nothing. Worse, the bloating got slightly more intense, which I told myself was the stomach "waking up." Day twenty-five I was still going four days between bowel movements. Day thirty-one my husband asked if I'd actually started the new thing the doctor recommended and I lied and said yes.

That weekend I called the apigenin company on the bottle. Asked them what the standardized apigenin content was per capsule.

The woman read me the label out loud.

Celery seed powder. 450mg per capsule. No standardized apigenin extract listed.

I asked her how much actual apigenin that was.

She didn't know. She put me on hold for ten minutes. Came back and said the company didn't disclose the standardized extract percentage. "It's a whole-food source," she said.

I went back to my notes from the appointment and found the article my gastroenterologist had emailed me afterward. The clinical research on apigenin and gastric motility used standardized apigenin extract at thirty to fifty milligrams of pure apigenin daily.

Less than zero point one percent of celery seed powder is actual apigenin.

I'd been taking maybe half a milligram of real apigenin a day.

Less than one one-hundredth of the clinical dose.

I sat at my kitchen table looking at three bottles I'd just spent forty-eight dollars on and I felt that same sick feeling I'd had at the colonoscopy two months earlier. Different aisle. Same problem. I'd outsmarted myself into wasting more time.

I thought about the gastroparesis patient. Three years. Six small things a day. Never going back.

I'd just given away another month.

The next morning I called my gastroenterologist's office. Left a message asking if there was a specific product she'd been talking about, because the ones I'd been finding on Amazon weren't working.

Her nurse called back that afternoon.

"She wanted me to tell you that's the exact reason she stopped letting patients piece it together themselves. She's been recommending one specific brand for about six months now. She vetted it because she got tired of watching patients buy underdosed celery capsules and chlorophyllin pills with no actual apigenin in them. She had a friend who runs a third-party supplement testing lab in Colorado test the top eighteen products on the market that claim to support GLP-1 digestion."

"And?"

"Fourteen of them tested under five milligrams of actual standardized apigenin per serving. Three had no detectable apigenin at all, just rice powder and binders. Two had heavy metal contamination above safe limits."

"How many passed?"

"One."

The brand was called Motilli. A small company that made a celery juice fiber gummy specifically for women on GLP-1 medications. Standardized apigenin extract. Not powder. Combined with chlorophyllin and a low-dose soluble prebiotic. The exact three-piece protocol she'd drawn out for me on the printout.

"She has a sister-in-law on Wegovy who's been on it for five months. That's the other reason she recommends it. She's watched it work in her own family."

I asked the nurse to text me the link.

She did.

I ordered it that night. Not because I was hopeful. I'd stopped being hopeful somewhere around bottle five. But because the woman who literally looked inside my stomach with a camera had vetted this one specifically. And they had a 90-day guarantee. So the worst that happens is I return it and I'm back where I was.

The first week I didn't notice much. Maybe slightly less pressure after dinner. I texted my sister that I was trying something new and she sent back the eye roll emoji. I'd told her that six times before.

Around day ten something shifted. I had a bowel movement that felt normal. Not forced. Not from a stimulant. Just my body doing what it used to do before Mounjaro.

I sat there for a second trying to remember the last time that happened on its own.

By week three the bloating changed. Not gone every single day. But not the unbutton-at-my-desk kind. I wore a fitted top on a Thursday without thinking about it. I don't know why I remember it was Thursday. I just remember looking down at lunch and realizing I hadn't reached for the cardigan.

At five weeks my husband said something at dinner. He said I seemed like myself again. That I wasn't pushing food around my plate or finding reasons to leave the table early.

I hadn't told him about the gummies.

He just noticed.

The Sunday after that I went to my sister's for dinner. Sat through the whole meal. Had seconds. Stayed for coffee after. First time in months I didn't once think about what was going to happen when I stood up from the table.

My sister asked if I'd changed my medication. I told her no. Same Mounjaro. Same dose.

I just stopped treating the wrong organ.

My daughter came over with the grandkids the following weekend. We made pancakes. I ate two. She didn't have to wait for me to come back to the conversation. We talked about the apple orchard trip and I listened to the whole thing without my body running its usual calculations.

She didn't say anything about it. She didn't need to. She just looked at me a few times during breakfast the way she used to look at me when I was the mother who showed up.

I think about those nine months sometimes. Seven bottles. Hundreds of dollars. Every morning standing at my bathroom counter trying to figure out which combination of colon products might help a stomach problem.

And then I think about those three weeks afterward. The forty-eight dollars I spent on three more bottles I didn't need because I thought I could outsmart the doctor and piece it together cheaper from Amazon.

Both of those mistakes cost me time I don't get back.

The woman who waited three years doesn't get hers back either.

If you're on a GLP-1 and nothing you're taking is working, please hear me on this part.

It is not the products. The products do exactly what their labels say. They just say it about an organ that isn't where your problem is.

And if you've already figured that out and you're now reaching for a celery capsule on Amazon, please pause. Standardized apigenin extract is not the same thing as ground-up celery seed in a pill. Whole-food source labeling is a way of not telling you the dose. The clinical research is on the standardized extract. Anything less is another month you don't get back.

There are two versions of the next ninety days for you.

In one of them, you keep buying laxatives. Or you order another generic celery capsule. Or you skip another Sunday dinner. Or you tell yourself this is just what the medication costs. And you wait. The way I waited. The way the woman who can't have a normal meal anymore waited.

In the other one, you give your stomach the actual three things it has been asking for, in the actual form your body can absorb, and you watch what happens between week one and week six.

That is the whole choice.

The link is below if you want it.

A few notes on what to expect.

They run a 90-day money-back guarantee on it, which is the only reason I tried it after I'd already wasted forty-eight dollars on the Amazon version. Anyone who has been told for nine months to add another laxative while their body refuses to work deserves to find out for themselves without losing anything else.

They batch-produce in small quantities because standardized apigenin extract degrades when it's exposed to light and heat for too long. The bottles sell out for stretches when more women in the GLP-1 groups find them. If you go to the link and the bottle is in stock, I would not wait until next week.

The medication that gave you back your jeans does not have to be the medication that takes away your dinner.

Apigenin for the stomach. Chlorophyllin for the gas. Prebiotic fiber for the colon. In a form you can actually absorb. At a dose the research is actually built on. Verified by a doctor who looked inside her patients' stomachs with a camera and got tired of watching them buy the wrong organ's medicine.

That is what I'd want my own daughter handed on day one if she ever told me she was starting one of these shots. So that is what I am handing you now.

P.S. About six weeks into the gummies, I asked my gastroenterologist at a follow-up about the patient she'd told me about. The one with gastroparesis. Three years in. Six small things a day. I asked if I could write to her. My gastroenterologist asked her, and she said yes. We've been emailing since. She told me last month that if I keep doing what I'm doing, my window stays open. She told me hers closed somewhere between year two and year three and nobody was telling her anything different than what my first six doctors told me. She also told me that if reading this gets one woman to skip the laxative aisle and start where the actual problem is, she wants her story out there. So her name is Carol. She used to be a high school principal in Naperville. She had a stomach exactly like yours nine months ago. She wants you to read this before another month goes by.

The link is below.
creative.title: "Your colon is healthy. That's not where your problem is."
